newsitem.title: portugal: OPINION - Portugal and EMU membership - By Vitor Bento.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Portugal and EMU membership - By Vitor Bento.

text.p: The following article was specially written for Reuters by Vitor Bento, president of the board at the Institute of Public Credit Management, the body responsible for managing Portugal's state debt.

Looking back to the achievements of a decade of membership of the European Union, what remains to be done for Portugal to meet the necessary convergence criteria on time to join EMU in 1999 is not extraordinary.
Therefore, counting Portugal as a starting member of Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) is not a daring bet. On the contrary, it looks a very feasible event.

The public deficit is now estimated at four percent of GDP (gross domestic product) in 1996, which compares favourably with Britain's, Austria's, France's or Germany's, for instance. The public debt ratio, although above the 60 percent (of GDP) reference value, is lower than Belgian's, Ireland's or the Netherlands' and is expected to show a steady decline in 1996 and 1997.

Long-term interest rates have already converged enough to be well within the limits set up by the (Maastricht) Treaty and, unless a spell of distrust affects the performance of the other criteria, are unlikely to diverge again significantly.

On the inflation front, there may be some difficulties because the process of real convergence (improving living standards) requires faster growth in non-tradable prices in Portugal than in richer countries. Also, because the deflation (or almost deflation) that some countries went through recently, lowered abnormally the reference value for this criteria.
Nonetheless, we remain convinced that meeeting this criteria is within reach for Portugal.
To sum up, one cannot say that meeting the convergence criteria on time will be an easy task for Portugal, but it can be honestly recognized that the task is feasible.

Indeed, it is not a more difficult task than the one faced by some other countries that are usually counted in. The political will seems to exist, together with the political and social conscience of the importance of such a strategic goal.

In spite of the unavoidable emergence of "contrariant" voices at the two extremes of the political spectrum, the large majority of the country seems to support the objective of participation in the EMU from the beginning, as can be derived from the results of the last elections.
The two parties that defended explicitly this objective collected almost 80 percent of the vote.

On the other hand, Portugal seems well equipped to face the challenges of the future single currency area. First, because the Portuguese economy has long been very open and used to foreign competition, as the country was a founding member of EFTA.
Second, because the economy underwent a major restructuring process since its accession to the former EEC that has improved significantly its productive fabric.

In fact, a stable current account, a stable trade deficit (in percentage of GDP), some improvements in the market share of exports and a more than 20 percent appreciation in the real exchange rate since 1985 can only be reconciled by fast productivity growth.

Thirdly, EMU, by giving up monetary policy and constraining the use of fiscal policy (through the recently agreed stability pact), will require a very flexible labour market and the Portuguese labour market is already recognized as one of the most flexible in the European Union (Portugal has shown consistently one of the lowest unemployment rates in the EU).
Therefore, Portugal seems to have reasons to look confidently to its early participation in the EMU.
